source.title: The Erdős-Ulam problem, Lang's conjecture, and uniformity

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a subset S of the Euclidean plane R^2 such that the distance between any two points of S is rational and S is dense in R^2 with respect to the usual Euclidean topology?

evidence.quote: A rational distance set is a subset S of R2 such that the distance between any two points of S is a rational number.
Question 1. Is there a rational distance set that is dense for the Euclidean topology of R2?
While this problem is still open, Shaﬀaf [ Sha18] and Tao [ Tao14] independently showed that Lang’s Conjecture (Conjecture 2.2 below) implies that the answer to the Erdős-Ulam question is ‘no’.

accepted.question_text: Let K be a number field and let X be a projective variety defined over K. If X is of general type, meaning that for any desingularization of X the canonical divisor of the desingularization is big, must the set X(K) of K-rational points fail to be Zariski dense in X?
accepted.context_brief: Lang's conjecture for varieties of general type

evidence.quote: Deﬁnition 2.1. A projective variety X is of general type if for any desingularization ˜X → X the canonical divisor ω ˜X is big.
Conjecture 2.2 (Lang’s Conjecture) . Let X be a projective variety of general type deﬁned over a number ﬁeld K. Then the set of rational points X(K) is not Zariski dense in X.
Conjecture 2.2 is known in full generality only for curves, where it reduces to Faltings’ Theorem [Fal83] and subvarieties of abelian varieties [ Fal91].

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a set S of seven points in R^2 such that every pairwise Euclidean distance between points of S is rational, no three points of S lie on one line, and no four points of S lie on one circle?
accepted.context_brief: Seven-point rational distance set in general position

evidence.quote: A rational distance set is a subset S of R2 such that the distance between any two points of S is a rational number.
For example, a set of seven points in R2 is in general position if and only if no 7 − 4 = 3 points lie on a line and no 7 − 3 = 4 points lie on a circle.
Erdős famously asked whether there exists a rational distance set with seven elements in general position.
Erdős’ question was answered in the aﬃrmative by Kreisel and Kurz [ KK08].

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a rational distance set S in R^2 in general position with more than seven elements, where rational distance means every pairwise Euclidean distance in S is rational and, for n = |S|, general position means no subset of S of cardinality n − 4 is contained in a line and no subset of S of cardinality n − 3 is contained in a circle?
accepted.context_brief: Rational distance sets in general position beyond seven points

evidence.quote: A rational distance set is a subset S of R2 such that the distance between any two points of S is a rational number.
we say a subset S ⊆ R2 of cardinality n is in general position if no subset of S of cardinality n − 4 is contained in a line and no subset of S of cardinality n − 3 is contained in a circle.
We are unaware of any examples of rational distance sets in general position of cardinality larger than seven.

accepted.question_text: Do there exist rational distance sets in R^2 in general position whose cardinalities are larger than any fixed constant, where a rational distance set has rational pairwise Euclidean distances and a finite set S of size n is in general position when no n − 4 of its points lie on one line and no n − 3 of its points lie on one circle?
accepted.context_brief: Unbounded cardinalities of rational distance sets in general position

evidence.quote: A rational distance set is a subset S of R2 such that the distance between any two points of S is a rational number.
we say a subset S ⊆ R2 of cardinality n is in general position if no subset of S of cardinality n − 4 is contained in a line and no subset of S of cardinality n − 3 is contained in a circle.
Corollary 1.2. If there exist rational distance sets in general position of cardinality larger than any ﬁxed constant, then Lang’s Conjecture does not hold.
